newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serbs torch homes of Moslem refugees.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs torch homes of Moslem refugees.

text.p: A Serb mob burned homes belonging to Moslem refugees trying to resettle their village in Serb-controlled territory this weekend, prompting heavy criticism of the NATO-led Bosnia peace force on Monday.
A mob of 150 Serbs entered a village patrolled by Russian peacekeeping troops and put 11 pre-fabricated houses to the torch on Sunday afternoon, the Stabilisation Force (SFOR) reported.
The remaining four houses constructed by Moslem refugees had been blown up earlier over the weekend.
As a result, the international peace force came under heavy criticism from Bosnian refugees.

Fadil Banjanovic, a leader of Moslem refugees in northeast Bosnia, expressed outrage that the NATO-led force could not protect 15 prefabricated homes which had been constructed under rules set down by SFOR and international agencies.
"If the international force tolerates these terroristic acts by Serb extremists then SFOR should pack up and leave Bosnia," Banjanovic told reporters in Tuzla.
SFOR said that the Russian troops found themselves in a difficult position and chose not to fire on the crowd.

"The Russian troops saw them coming and did the best they could under the circumstances. Bear in mind there were 150 Serbs and approximately 20 Russian soldiers," spokesman Major Andrew Saddleton told a news conference in Sarajevo.

"The only way of stopping these people was to use lethal force. The commander on the ground made a decision not to use lethal force and at no time were innocent civilians, SFOR troops or SFOR equipment under threat."

But Moslem officials said refugees from Gajevi have submitted to a vetting procedure conducted by SFOR and international agencies in the belief that peace force troops would provide safe conditions for their return.
"We will ask of those who have the weapons and who could have stopped it to pay damages to the people whose homes have been burned," said Sead Jamagosmanovic, governor of the Tuzla canton.
NATO and the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) says it is up to the local Serb police -- and not peacekeeping troops -- to ensure security in Gajevi.

After a firefight erupted in Gajevi last October, NATO announced it was stepping up patrols and other security measures to deter further violence in villages lying near the boundary between Serb and Moslem-Croat territories.
By laying mines and booby-traps, Serbs have violated a NATO ban on weapons in the area, which is located within the "Zone of Separation" along a former front line.

"We condemn the failure of the (Serb republic) police to uphold and enforce the law as agreed by all sides and for not adhering to the return procedure," said Colum Murphy, a spokesman for the international High Representative to Bosnia.
The major powers' Contact Group on former Yugoslavia was due to discuss tensions in Gajevi and the southern town of Mostar in a meeting in Brussels on Monday, Murphy said.
Sunday's incident appeared to be in retaliation for the abduction of three Serbs by Moslem-Croat federation authorities over the weekend, international police monitors said.
Two men and a woman were held on Friday night and international police monitors said they had been beaten while under detention.
The report of the abduction came after a Moslem man was detained a few days earlier for allegedly carrying a shotgun inside Serb territory.
